title: "Getting started with CDCAtlas"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
```

**CDCAtlas** provides R functions for retrieving public health surveillance data
from CDC AtlasPlus.

This article introduces common use patterns:

- retrieving national, state- and county-level data
- querying different diseases
- using sex, age, and race/ethnicity stratification
- comparing rates across groups
- preparing AtlasPlus data for plotting and analysis

This article does **not** cover tract-level extrapolation. That is an advanced
use case covered in
[Extrapolation to tracts](extrapolation.html).

## Installation

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("VagishHemmige/CDCAtlas")
```

## Setup

```{r}
library(CDCAtlas)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Basic query: state-level chlamydia data

A simple query retrieves one disease, one geography level, and one year.

```{r}
chlamydia_state <- get_atlas(
  disease   = "chlamydia",
  geography = "state",
  year      = 2022
)

head(chlamydia_state)
```

The returned object is a data frame that can be used directly with tidyverse
tools. Each row is one indicator, place, year and stratum; the `indicator`
column says what was counted, and `data_status` says whether a value is
suppressed or not available.

```{r}
glimpse(chlamydia_state)
```

## Plot state-level rates

AtlasPlus's state level also includes U.S. territories. Their FIPS codes are
above 56, so this keeps the 50 states and the District of Columbia:

```{r}
is_state_or_dc <- function(fips) as.integer(fips) <= 56
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Bar chart of 2022 chlamydia rates per 100,000 population for the 50 states and DC, sorted from highest to lowest."}
chlamydia_state |>
  filter(is_state_or_dc(fips), !is.na(rate100000)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(geography, rate100000), y = rate100000)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Chlamydia rate by state and DC, 2022",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Rate per 100,000"
  )
```

## Query county-level data

AtlasPlus can also return county-level data for supported diseases.

```{r}
chlamydia_county <- get_atlas(
  disease   = "chlamydia",
  geography = "county",
  year      = 2022
)

head(chlamydia_county)
```

A common workflow is to identify counties with the highest reported rates.

```{r}
chlamydia_county |>
  filter(!is.na(rate100000)) |>
  arrange(desc(rate100000)) |>
  select(geography, cases, rate100000) |>
  head(10)
```

## Stratification by sex

Many AtlasPlus endpoints support stratification. For example, we can retrieve
state-level gonorrhea data by sex.

```{r}
gonorrhea_sex <- get_atlas(
  disease   = "gonorrhea",
  geography = "state",
  year      = 2022,
  stratify_by = "sex"
)

head(gonorrhea_sex)
```

Now we can compare rates by sex within each state.

```{r, fig.alt = "Two bar charts, one per sex, of the ten states or DC with the highest 2022 gonorrhea rates per 100,000 population."}
gonorrhea_sex |>
  filter(is_state_or_dc(fips), !is.na(rate100000)) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  slice_max(rate100000, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(geography, rate100000), y = rate100000)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ sex, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "States (and DC) with the highest gonorrhea rates by sex, 2022",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Rate per 100,000"
  )
```

## Stratification by age

AtlasPlus also supports age-stratified queries for many disease/geography
combinations. For national figures, ask for `geography = "national"` rather
than adding up states: CDC's national totals don't depend on which state cells
are suppressed, and state rows include territories.

```{r}
hiv_age <- get_atlas(
  disease   = "hiv",
  geography = "national",
  year      = 2022,
  stratify_by = "age"
)

hiv_age |>
  select(indicator, age, cases, rate100000)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Bar chart of 2022 U.S. HIV diagnoses by age group."}
hiv_age |>
  filter(indicator == "HIV diagnoses") |>
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x = age, y = cases)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "HIV diagnoses by age group, United States, 2022",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Cases"
  )
```

## Stratification by race/ethnicity

CDC AtlasPlus commonly uses a combined race/ethnicity variable rather than
separate race and Hispanic ethnicity fields.

```{r}
hiv_race <- get_atlas(
  disease     = "hiv",
  geography   = "national",
  year        = 2022,
  stratify_by = "race"
)

hiv_race |>
  select(indicator, race_ethnicity, cases, rate100000) |>
  arrange(indicator, desc(cases))
```

Cases with unknown race/ethnicity are counted in the totals but not shown by
race, so the groups may not add up to the total.

```{r, fig.alt = "Bar chart of 2022 U.S. HIV diagnoses by race and ethnicity, sorted from most to fewest."}
hiv_race |>
  filter(indicator == "HIV diagnoses") |>
  ggplot(mapping =aes(x = reorder(race_ethnicity, cases), y = cases)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "HIV diagnoses by race/ethnicity, United States, 2022",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Cases"
  )
```

## Multiple stratification variables

You can request combinations of stratification variables when supported by the
underlying AtlasPlus endpoint. For example, HIV data can be queried by both sex
and age.

```{r}
hiv_age_sex <- get_atlas(
  disease     = "hiv",
  geography   = "national",
  year        = 2022,
  stratify_by = c("sex", "age")
)

hiv_age_sex |>
  select(indicator, sex, age, cases)
```

This allows direct comparison of age distributions by sex.

```{r, fig.alt = "Two bar charts, one per sex, of 2022 U.S. HIV diagnoses by age group."}
hiv_age_sex |>
  filter(indicator == "HIV diagnoses") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = cases)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(
    title = "HIV diagnoses by age and sex, United States, 2022",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Cases"
  )
```

## Comparing years

You can also query multiple years and compare trends over time. AtlasPlus
warns that "due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, data for 2020 and 2021
may need to be interpreted with caution"
([AtlasPlus](https://gis.cdc.gov/grasp/nchhstpatlas/main.html)), so read
changes across those years carefully.

```{r}
syphilis_trend <- get_atlas(
  disease   = "adult syphilis",
  geography = "national",
  year      = 2018:2022
)

syphilis_trend |>
  select(year, indicator, cases, rate100000)
```

`"adult syphilis"` returns one indicator per stage.

```{r, fig.alt = "Line chart of U.S. adult syphilis cases from 2018 to 2022, one line per stage."}
syphilis_trend |>
ggplot(mapping= aes(x = year, y = cases, color=indicator, group=indicator)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Adult syphilis cases by stage, United States, 2018-2022",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Cases"
  )
```

## Working with censored or missing values

CDC AtlasPlus may suppress or censor some values, especially for small counts.
Depending on the disease and geography, `cases` or `rate100000` may be missing.
`data_status` says why.

A common first step is to inspect missingness.

```{r}
chlamydia_county |>
  summarize(
    n_rows = n(),
    missing_cases = sum(is.na(cases)),
    missing_rates = sum(is.na(rate100000))
  )

chlamydia_county |>
  count(data_status)
```

Recent years can also be provisional. For HIV, AtlasPlus's technical notes say
data are preliminary until a 12-month reporting delay has passed and shouldn't
be used for formal trend analyses until then. Check the technical notes for each
indicator (in the AtlasPlus menu) before comparing years.


## Choosing diseases, geographies and strata

`get_atlas()` takes one of eight `disease` values. Each returns several
indicators (see `?get_atlas`), and AtlasPlus offers each at different
geographies:

| `disease` | Geographies | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `"hiv"` | national, state, county, msa | HIV diagnoses and prevalence |
| `"estimate"` | national, region, state, county | Estimated HIV incidence and prevalence, and Knowledge of Status |
| `"chlamydia"`, `"gonorrhea"`, `"adult syphilis"` | national, state, county | Age groups include "Unknown" |
| `"tuberculosis"` | national, state, county | |
| `"hepatitis"` | national, state | No county data |
| `"congenital syphilis"` | national, state | Can't be stratified |

`get_atlas()` stops with an error, before downloading, when CDC doesn't offer
what is asked for.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
get_atlas(disease = "estimate", geography = "region", year = 2021)
get_atlas(disease = "hepatitis", geography = "state", year = 2022)
get_atlas(disease = "tuberculosis", geography = "county", year = 2022)
```

Each disease has its own age groups: 13-24 to 65+ for `"hiv"` and
`"estimate"`, and 0-14 to 65+ for the others except congenital syphilis. [About CDC AtlasPlus
data](about-atlasplus-data.html) lists them, with what CDC's numbers mean and
where they trip people up.


## Saved downloads

Each response from CDC is saved on your computer and reused for 30 days, so
running the same code again doesn't download the data again. To download
fresh data sooner, for example after CDC revises a recent year:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
get_atlas(disease = "chlamydia", geography = "county", year = 2022, refresh = TRUE)

# Or delete every saved download
clear_atlas_cache()
```

See `?get_atlas` for full argument documentation.
